rv.q: Mary is such an original character and Shaw such a master at the art of creative shock, that in the process of delivering her testimony, one traditional legend after another is smashed to bits.
Her fierce virtuosity transforms Tóibín’s extended monologue into a full-blooded theatrical portrait.
With both enormous audacity and bottomless grief, Tóibín's 90-minute stunner imagines a version of the Christ story "from the silent woman we pray to."
Here the script they’re working with isn’t nearly as remarkable — but Shaw’s charismatic, almost possessed performance is.
In purporting to tell a “real” story of Mary, Colm Tóibín’s play necessarily puts the New Testament matriarch in several contexts, one of which is death.
But the play’s bitter final words on redemption and its cost are its most devastating.
The combined effect of all this stuff is faint indeed, a playful obliqueness that seems somewhat pointless.
That it doesn’t quite work out that way ranks as one of the greater disappointments in a season that has made a practice of dashing hopes.
Colm Tóibín's spare, poetic monologue gets a respectful but static staging that doesn't fully capitalize on Fiona Shaw's formidable talents.
But, as Mary, Fiona Shaw ignites and glows with a fevered intensity and intelligence in this bold and indelibly theatrical work.
Fiona Shaw gives a performance of such towering intensity and commitment that it transcends the material's inherent limitations and creates something approaching theatrical magic.
Beyond all that, though, Shaw delivers a rich, often affecting portrayal of a woman who has lost her child amid a cosmic shift in the world she neither wants nor understands.

For all its eloquence and emotional range, in fact, Toibin's play lacks a certain dramatic dynamism; it's actually more compelling to read than to watch, even in the hands of so formidable a leading lady.
Under the direction of Deborah Warner, Shaw delivers a raw, raging performance.
Similarly, Shaw’s vocal mannerisms and dramatic use of physicality increasingly seem not only imposed and inorganic but also repetitive.
